analysis.one_liner: Lets the government's investigative arm audit the Federal Reserve's emergency credit facilities and report findings to Congress.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let Congress's investigative arm audit the Fed's crisis credit facilities, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: During the financial crisis, the Federal Reserve set up special lending programs — with names like the Term Auction Facility and the Primary Dealer Credit Facility — that the government's investigative arm, the Comptroller General, is largely barred from auditing under existing law. This bill would have changed that, letting the Comptroller General examine those facilities, their records, and their staff, and report the findings to Congress, with the authority expiring after five years. It never got a hearing or a vote; it was sent to the Senate Banking Committee and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and ordinary citizens gain an independent, outside accounting of who received trillions in emergency central bank lending and on what terms. The Federal Reserve's emergency facilities created after the 2008 crisis were largely shielded from GAO examination under existing law; this bill would have pried open their books — including the special purpose vehicles used to make the loans — and required public reports to Congress. Workers and savers who ultimately bear the risk when the central bank backstops big finance would finally see who got the help.

how_it_helps.text: It would have given the Comptroller General full access to the records, property, and personnel of every Fed crisis lending facility, including special purpose vehicles.
It required a public report to Congress with findings and recommendations within 90 days of each review, so the results could not simply be buried.
It would have overridden the statutory limits in current law that shield certain Federal Reserve functions from audit, at least for the named emergency facilities.

analysis.who_pays: The Federal Reserve and the banks and financial firms that used its emergency credit facilities would face exposure: auditors naming who borrowed, how much, and on what terms. Financial institutions argue that such exposure can create stigma and market disruption during a crisis.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Fed and its borrower banks

drawbacks.text: Opponents of Federal Reserve audits have long argued that letting investigators name institutions that borrow from emergency lending facilities can itself rattle markets — banks may hesitate to use the lender of last resort for fear of the stigma, making panics worse.
The bill included a built-in five-year sunset, so even had it passed, the audit authority would have expired and needed reauthorization.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — an independent government check on trillions in emergency Fed lending — was real and low-cost, since the GAO already exists and the sunset limited the burden. The main counterargument, made by the Fed and financial-sector defenders, was that exposure of which institutions borrowed during a panic could itself unsettle markets and discourage banks from using emergency backstops in the next crisis. Whether that risk outweighs transparency was the fight in this era; this bill never got a chance to test it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never came up again before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 15, 2009 by Senator Susan Collins.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was recorded in the 111th Congress: no committee markup, no floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

Meanwhile, the emergency facilities the bill named — including the Term Auction Facility, Primary Dealer Credit Facility, and Commercial Paper Funding Facility — continued to operate beyond independent audit review under existing law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Federal Reserve's institutional confidentiality, and the banks and financial firms that had used its emergency credit facilities, were better off because the bill never moved — the details of who received crisis lending stayed outside GAO reach.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Fed and its borrower banks

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, proposing to give the Comptroller General audit power over Federal Reserve emergency credit facilities.

for.name: 1 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 15, 2009 and took no recorded action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor, but with no votes ever taken, no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped the Fed's statutory exemption from GAO examination for its emergency credit facilities and required public reporting on who received crisis lending. The Fed's institutional preference for confidentiality in lender-of-last-resort operations would have ended.

industries.industry: Banks and Wall Street financial institutions
industries.note: These were the recipients of the emergency facilities the bill targeted. Full audit could have exposed which firms received crisis support and on what terms, threatening the confidentiality many borrowers valued. At the same time, greater confidence in a supervised Fed could support financial stability that benefits the sector.
